stories.detail: SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- With a bye week coming soon, San Francisco 49ers receiver Mike Evans and defensive end Nick Bosa won't play in Sunday's game against the Atlanta Falcons as they deal with Achilles tendinitis and a calf injury, respectively. On Friday, the Niners ruled Evans and Bosa out against the Falcons after neither player participated in practice this week. In addition to Bosa and Evans, the Niners also ruled out wideout Deebo Samuel Sr. (hamstring), linebackers Luke Gifford (groin) and Garret Wallow (hamstring) and safety Marques Sigle (ankle). Coach Kyle Shanahan said that with so many missing players, the Niners are likely to enter Sunday's game with fewer than the maximum 48 players on the game day roster even after they make practice squad elevations on Saturday. They've had internal discussions with some of their players about further injuries forcing them to play out of position, according to Shanahan. "I don't think ever in my career (has that happened," Shanahan said. "It's a unique situation." stories.title: Falcons' viral stripes will appear down center of helmets
stories.summary: A vertical stripe pattern that the Falcons used in a social media post will appear down the middle of the team's throwback helmets. The stripes drew significant online backlash as some saw similarity to Nazi Germany imagery.
stories.detail: FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- The Atlanta Falcons posted a rendering of their throwback logo Wednesday on social media that created an online backlash, with some posters comparing it to imagery found in Nazi Germany. The post featured the franchise's throwback black-and-white bird logo, which it used from the 1960s all the way up to the early 2000s. Behind the logo were vertical stripes in red, black and gold. The colors are a reference to the team's 1966 uniform, which consisted of a red helmet, the black Falcons logo, and black, white and gold striping on the pants. The Falcons' post remains up , but the team changed its X and Instagram profile photos to one with just the red retro helmet with the black throwback logo on it and no vertical stripes. The Falcons have worn the retro logo for games every year since 2009 with the exception of several years when the NFL prevented teams from using an alternative helmet color. Atlanta will wear the logo Sunday when it hosts the San Francisco 49ers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The presentation of the retro logo on top of the vertical striping in those colors on that specific social media post seems to be the object of controversy. The stripes will…

stories.detail: FRISCO, Texas -- At 2-4 and in the midst of a two-game losing streak, Dak Prescott knows it is time for the Dallas Cowboys to turn the season around. stories.title: Cam Skattebo set to return to Giants RB mix after being 'taught a lesson'
stories.summary: After zero carries in Week 6, Cam Skattebo says he took a step back to evaluate and correct, and Giants' coach says he should return to the running back mix vs. the Texans.
stories.detail: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- Cam Skattebo had a "good week" of practice and should return to the running back mix for the New York Giants against the Houston Texans , coach John Harbaugh said Friday. Skattebo didn't have a single carry in Sunday's 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints . He landed on the bench for most of last week's game after a crucial overtime fumble in a tie with the Washington Commanders . It was his fifth fumble in 13 career games. "It's been good, you know. I think I got taught a lesson," Skattebo said. "I don't know if that's from them or from myself, but I kind of had to step back and look at it and figure out why I was doing the things I was doing, what was happening. Came to practice, corrected those things, worked on them. Ready to go back out there and play ball." The Giants had Najee Harris , who was released Tuesday , Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary ahead of Skattebo in the rotation against the Saints. Skattebo played six snaps after averaging 42 over the first five games. The Giants praised Skattebo this week for handling it like a "pro" and trying to correct the mistakes. stories.title: NFL admits a penalty by the Cowboys in Week 5 was assessed against the Bucs
stories.summary: The NFL has admitted a rather embarrassing officiating mistake from Week 5: When Buccaneers defensive lineman Calijah Kancey was called for illegal hands to the face, it was actually a Cowboys player who put his hands in Kancey's face, and somehow the wrong team got assessed the penalty when it was…
stories.detail: The NFL has admitted a rather embarrassing officiating mistake from Week 5: When Buccaneers defensive lineman Calijah Kancey was called for illegal hands to the face, it was actually a Cowboys player who put his hands in Kancey's face, and somehow the wrong team got assessed the penalty when it was time to step off the yardage. In the weekly officiating video , NFL officiating and rules analyst Walt Anderson said Cowboys guard Tyler Booker put his hands in Kancey's face but somehow that was miscommunicated as Kancey committing the penalty. Anderson said when the on-field officials make a mistake that blatant, the league officiating office should correct it immediately. "Were going to have a foul called on No. 94 on the defensive team for illegal hands to the face," Anderson said. "The only action relative to any hands is really by the offensive player here. So this is the type of play that the Competition Committee has instructed officiating that if objective information in terms of just asking the officials, 'Are we sure we have the right number of the player here?' that we can end up assisting with this. Because it's clearly not a foul by No. 94. If there is illegal use of hands…

stories.title: Knicks call plan to use fake championship rings as employee phishing test 'an unfortunate mistake,' will issue rings to employees
stories.summary: A spokesperson said the organization will be giving rings and jewelry to players, coaches and employees after report of the cybersecurity test went public.
stories.detail: The New York Knicks appear to be pivoting after a report that the team used the promise of championship rings as a cybersecurity test . In a statement to Yahoo Sports on Friday, a spokesperson for Madison Square Garden (MSG) confirmed a report from The Athletic that the company had sent emails last month offering employees championship rings as a phishing test. The company said it had recently undergone a hack, which led to the test, likely under the urging of Knicks owner James Dolan, who is known to be worried about cybersecurity. "The company had previously sent out an email to its corporate team as a simulation of a phishing attack designed to strengthen our security against hackers," the spokesman said. "MSG was recently hacked and extorted using an employee login and password obtained through a similar phishing attack. Using the rings as a lure to gain employees attention was an unfortunate mistake." Part of the oddness of the targeted phishing test is that, as The Athletic reported, many longtime MSG employees were not going to be receiving rings at all. That includes some who work in the Knicks' business operations — a role that would typically result in receiving a ring. …

Trade rumors, contract negotiations and free agency decisions can alter championship races and reshape the landscape of the entire league. This past offseason saw incredible movement , with some of the biggest stars in the game switching teams via free agency and trades. stories.title: Phishing email to Knicks employees an 'unfortunate mistake,' MSG spokesman says
stories.summary: A Madison Square Garden spokesman admitted fault that employees in Knicks business operations and at the arena received a phishing email posing as an opportunity to claim an NBA championship ring, calling the incident "an unfortunate mistake."
stories.detail: A Madison Square Garden spokesperson admitted fault that employees in Knicks business operations and at the arena received a phishing email posing as an opportunity to claim an NBA championship ring, calling the incident "an unfortunate mistake." The Athletic reported Thursday that some employees received an email last month saying "your Employee Championship Ring is here" that said they could choose from a pair of options at "no cost to you." When the employees clicked on a link in the email, The Athletic reported, they were informed that they had failed a phishing test and would have to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class. "The company had previously sent out an email to its corporate team as a simulation of a phishing attack designed to strengthen our security against hackers," the MSG spokesman said in a statement Friday. "MSG was recently hacked and extorted using an employee login and password obtained through a similar phishing attack. Using the rings as a lure to gain employees attention was an unfortunate mistake."
